**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2021. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer any FOUR questions. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées d'après les notions classiques du programme de Géologie A Level, sans source consultable. Les faits locaux (Cameroun, mont Cameroun) sont formulés avec prudence et sont à faire relire par un géologue avant mise en avant.

Points : 4 x 3 + 6 + 7 = 25, conformes au sujet. Pour 5(a) le sujet imprime 3 points par sous-partie (i) à (iv) mais pas le total du bloc : `points` de 5(a) = 12 (somme). Le sujet imprime « (7 mark) » pour 5(c) : coquille, lu comme 7 points.

5(a) : « preservation potential of rocks » est lu comme la capacité de la roche à conserver des fossiles (sens usuel en paléontologie). Si le jury entendait la résistance de la roche à l'érosion, la réponse serait à adapter.
5(b) : exemples miniers cités (Chuquicamata au Chili, Witwatersrand en Afrique du Sud) donnés comme repères généraux ; aucune statistique.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Discuss the preservation potentials of the following rocks:

(i) Igneous rocks;  (3 marks)

(ii) Metamorphic rocks;  (3 marks)

(iii) Fine-grained clastic sedimentary rocks;  (3 marks)

(iv) Coarse-grained clastic sedimentary rocks.  (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **preservation potential** of a rock is its ability to preserve the **remains of organisms (fossils)** after burial, and it depends on how the rock formed (temperature, pressure, grain size, energy of the environment) and on what happens to it afterwards.

**(i) Igneous rocks: very low (almost nil).** Intrusive rocks form from molten magma at 650 to 1 200 degrees Celsius, which burns or destroys any organic remains, and their interlocking crystals leave no space for fossils. Only **extrusive volcanic rocks** may preserve a few fossils: the moulds of trees or animals engulfed by lava, and the remains buried by **volcanic ash (tuff)**, which can preserve delicate structures (leaf prints, footprints, and even whole bodies, as at Pompeii).

**(ii) Metamorphic rocks: poor.** The heat, the pressure and the recrystallisation of metamorphism **destroy, distort or obliterate** fossils; the higher the grade, the less chance, so that high-grade rocks (gneiss, schist) contain none. Fossils may survive only in **low-grade rocks** such as slate (deformed graptolites and trilobites, stretched and flattened by the tectonic stress) and in marble (a few ghost-like shells and corals).

**(iii) Fine-grained clastic sedimentary rocks (shale, mudstone, siltstone, clay): excellent (the best).** They are deposited in **quiet, low-energy water** (lakes, lagoons, deep sea, swamps), where the remains are not broken by currents and are **buried quickly** by fine mud. The very fine grains record **fine detail** (soft parts, leaf and insect prints, graptolites, fish and carbon films); the low permeability limits the circulation of oxygenated water, and in **organic-rich, oxygen-poor muds (black shales)** decay is slow (the exceptional preservation of Lagerstatten, such as the Burgess Shale). Their weakness is flattening by compaction.

**(iv) Coarse-grained clastic sedimentary rocks (sandstone, conglomerate): poor to fair.** They are deposited in **high-energy environments** (rivers, beaches, dunes), where shells and bones are **broken, abraded and sorted**, and the **high porosity and permeability** allow circulating groundwater to **dissolve shells** (especially aragonite, leaving moulds and casts) and to bring oxygen, which causes decay. The fossils are therefore usually fragmentary and coarse, preserved as **moulds, casts, wood, bone beds, trace fossils (burrows, footprints, trackways)**, with little fine detail.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Discuss TWO methods of mining.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Mining is the extraction of rocks and minerals of economic value from the ground. Two methods are discussed: **surface (open-cast) mining** and **underground mining**.

**1. Surface mining (open-pit or open-cast mining, and quarrying).** The overburden (soil and waste rock) is removed, often in **benches or terraces**, and the ore or rock is dug, drilled, blasted and carted away from the open pit. Alluvial and strip mining are other surface methods.
- *Used when* the deposit is **at or near the surface, large and of low grade** (porphyry copper, iron ore, bauxite, coal seams close to the surface, building stone, limestone for cement, gravel and sand).
- *Advantages:* **cheap per tonne**, large machines may be used, a high recovery of the ore, a better safety and an easy ventilation; the output is large.
- *Disadvantages:* a large area of land is destroyed, there is **dust, noise, water pollution, scars and waste heaps**, the pit may fill with water, and the depth that can be worked is limited by the cost of removing the overburden (stripping ratio). Examples: Chuquicamata copper (Chile) and the limestone quarries for cement in many countries.

**2. Underground mining (shaft mining, adit or drift mining).** Access to the deposit is by a **vertical shaft**, or by an **inclined or horizontal tunnel (adit, drift)** on the side of a hill; the ore is removed by **stoping** or by **room and pillar** or **longwall** methods, and brought to the surface in cages and skips, with ventilation, pumping and roof supports.
- *Used when* the deposit is **deep, thin or steeply dipping, and of high grade** (gold and diamond mines, deep coal seams, rock salt, metal veins). Examples: the very deep gold mines of the Witwatersrand in South Africa.
- *Advantages:* the **surface is little disturbed**, deep ore bodies can be reached, and there is less waste.
- *Disadvantages:* it is **expensive** and slow, and dangerous (roof falls, explosions of gas, flooding, dust, heat), it needs pumping and ventilation, and **subsidence** may happen at the surface; part of the ore is left behind as pillars.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Explain the factors that will determine the quantity of ground water.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Groundwater is the water that fills the pores and fractures of the rocks below the **water table**. The quantity of groundwater that is stored and available depends on the following factors.

1. **Amount, intensity and seasonal distribution of the rainfall (recharge).** The water that enters the ground (infiltration) comes from the precipitation, so that areas with high and regular rainfall store more groundwater. Gentle, long rains give more infiltration than heavy showers, which run off. A rainy season followed by a dry season makes the water table rise and fall.
2. **Porosity of the rocks.** The volume of the voids (pores and cracks) determines how much water can be stored: the porosity of sand and gravel is 25 to 40 per cent, and that of clay is high but the pores are very small, so that the water is held and cannot be removed.
3. **Permeability of the rocks.** It is the ability to **transmit water** through connected pores and fractures: sandstone, sand, gravel and fractured or cavernous limestone are permeable (**aquifers**), and clay, shale and unfractured crystalline rocks are impermeable (**aquicludes**). A thick permeable aquifer stores and yields more water.
4. **Geological structure.** Joints, faults and bedding planes allow the water to enter and move; a **syncline or basin** collects the water, and an aquifer between two impermeable beds gives a **confined (artesian) aquifer** under pressure. The dip of the beds controls the area where recharge occurs.
5. **Relief and slope.** On steep slopes, the water **runs off quickly** and little infiltrates; on flat or gently sloping land and in valleys, the water stays longer and infiltrates more, so that the groundwater is more abundant.
6. **Vegetation and soil cover.** A cover of vegetation and a porous soil **slow down runoff** and favour infiltration with the roots, although the plants also use some water in transpiration; bare, compacted or paved ground (towns) reduces the infiltration.
7. **Climate: evaporation and temperature.** In hot dry regions, a large part of the water evaporates before it enters the ground, and in cold regions the ground may be frozen; both reduce the recharge.
8. **Human activities (abstraction).** If the water is **pumped out faster than it is recharged**, the water table falls; and the clearing of forests, urbanisation and the building of dams change the recharge. The **depth of the water table** and the size of the catchment area also determine the quantity.
